lead: Real machine parts rarely carry one stress. A shaft with a pulley has bending and torsion at the same point. A bracket with an offset load has direct stress and bending stress. Superposition adds these stresses at a point into a two-dimensional stress state. Principal stresses are the largest and smallest normal stresses on rotated planes; they show where a brittle part may crack or a ductile part may yield. This chapter combines stresses, converts eccentric loads into a direct force plus a moment, and finds principal stresses with a formula and Mohr's circle.
prereq: You need 1.6 for the direct, bending and torsion stress equations.

blocks.text: Superposition works when the material stays linear elastic and deflections are small. At a chosen point, take a small square element. Its faces show a normal stress σ and a shear stress τ. The subscript x means the face normal to the x-axis. Tensile σ is positive; compressive σ is negative.

blocks.where: P is axial force (N); A is cross-sectional area (mm²); M is bending moment (N·mm); y is distance from the neutral axis (mm); I is second moment of area (mm⁴). Use + where bending tension adds to axial tension.
T is torque (N·mm); r is radial distance from the axis (mm); J is polar second moment of area (mm⁴). At the surface r = d/2, so for a solid round shaft τ = 16T/(πd³).

blocks.text: For a solid round shaft of diameter d, bending gives σ<sub>x</sub> = 32M/(πd³) and torsion gives τ = 16T/(πd³). These two stresses act on the same surface element. There is no axial force in the simple shaft case, so σ<sub>y</sub> = 0. The element is in plane stress. If an axial force also acts, add P/A to σ<sub>x</sub> with its sign. Transverse shear stress is usually small at the surface; check it when the span is short.

An eccentric load is a force whose line of action misses the centroid of the section. Move the force to the centroid. This adds a moment M = P e, where P is the force (N) and e is the offset (mm). The member now has a direct stress P/A and a bending stress M c/I. The two stresses add on one side and subtract on the other. The maximum normal stress is σ<sub>max</sub> = P/A + P e c/I, where c is the distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre (mm).

Example. A 40 mm wide, 10 mm thick tie bar carries 20 kN with the line of action 15 mm from the centroidal axis along the width. A = 40 × 10 = 400 mm². Direct stress = 20 000/400 = 50 MPa. M = 20 000 × 15 = 300 000 N·mm. I = 10 × 40³/12 = 53 333 mm⁴; c = 20 mm. Bending stress = 300 000 × 20 / 53 333 = 112.5 MPa. Maximum = 50 + 112.5 = 162.5 MPa on the side where the moment causes tension. The other side has 50 − 112.5 = −62.5 MPa, i.e. compression.

The same rule applies to a bracket, a column, or a bolted joint. If the load is offset in two directions, use two moments and add biaxial bending. Eccentric bolted and welded joints are treated in Unit 4. The key point: never use P/A alone when the force is offset.

At a point, rotate the element by an angle θ. The normal stress σ and shear stress τ change. The planes where τ = 0 are principal planes. The normal stresses there are principal stresses σ₁ and σ₂. They are the largest and smallest normal stresses at that point. For plane stress with σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> and τ<sub>xy</sub>:

blocks.where: σ₁ is the algebraically larger principal stress; σ₂ is the smaller (it may be negative); σ<sub>x</sub> and σ<sub>y</sub> are normal stresses on x and y faces (MPa); τ<sub>xy</sub> is shear stress on those faces (MPa).
τ<sub>max</sub> is the maximum in-plane shear stress (MPa). The principal planes are at θ<sub>p</sub> = ½ tan⁻¹(2τ<sub>xy</sub>/(σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)).

blocks.text: For a shaft with bending and torsion only, σ<sub>y</sub> = 0. Then σ<sub>1,2</sub> = σ<sub>x</sub>/2 ± √((σ<sub>x</sub>/2)² + τ²). A useful check: σ₁ + σ₂ = σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>. The sum is invariant.

Mohr's circle draws this graphically. Centre C = ((σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2, 0). Radius R = √(((σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + τ<sub>xy</sub>²). The circle cuts the σ-axis at σ₁ and σ₂. The highest and lowest points have τ = ±τ<sub>max</sub>. Use the circle to see signs and planes quickly.

Strength check: compare σ₁ with the allowable tensile stress for a brittle material. For a ductile material, compare an equivalent stress from a yield theory; see Unit 2. Some syllabi call this whole calculation principal stresses for load combinations.

figure.caption: An offset force is split into a direct stress and a bending moment; the maximum normal stress is on the side where they add. The same flow applies to the shaft example, with bending and torsion instead of direct stress and bending.

spec.title: Eccentric load to principal stress
spec.aria: An eccentric load is split into direct and bending stresses; these form a stress state whose principal stresses are found and checked.

examples.question: A 50 mm diameter solid shaft transmits 15 kW at 300 rpm and carries a bending moment of 800 N·m. Find the torsional shear stress, the bending stress at the surface and the two principal stresses. Use π = 3.142.
steps: Bending stress σ<sub>x</sub> = M/Z = 800/(1.227 × 10⁻⁵) = 65.18 × 10⁶ Pa = 65.18 MPa.
Torsional shear stress τ = 16T/(πd³) = 16 × 477.4/(3.142 × 0.050³) = 19.45 × 10⁶ Pa = 19.45 MPa.
For σ<sub>y</sub> = 0: average = σ<sub>x</sub>/2 = 32.59 MPa. Radius R = √(32.59² + 19.45²) = 37.95 MPa.
examples.answer: The bending stress is 65.18 MPa, the torsional shear stress is 19.45 MPa, and the principal stresses are σ₁ = 70.54 MPa and σ₂ = −5.36 MPa; τ<sub>max</sub> = 37.95 MPa.
examples.check:
import math
P=15000.0
N=300.0
M=800.0
d=0.050
pi=3.142
T=P/(2*pi*N/60)
Z=pi*d**3/32
sigma_b=M/Z/1e6
tau=16*T/(pi*d**3)/1e6
avg=sigma_b/2
R=math.sqrt(avg**2+tau**2)
sigma1=avg+R
sigma2=avg-R
print(f'{sigma_b:.2f}')
print(f'{tau:.2f}')
print(f'{sigma1:.2f}')
print(f'{sigma2:.2f}')
print(f'{R:.2f}')

traps: Adding σ₁ to τ. Principal stresses are normal stresses on planes with zero shear; do not add a principal stress and a shear stress as if they were on the same plane.
Forgetting the moment P e in an eccentric load. A force offset from the centroid always gives both P/A and M c/I.
Using mm and m in the same formula. Convert torque to N·mm or diameter to m; 1 MPa = 1 N/mm².
Dropping the negative sign of σ₂. A compressive principal stress can control a brittle part; keep the sign.
Comparing τ<sub>max</sub> directly with tensile allowable stress without a failure theory. Use Unit 2 for ductile materials.

quiz.q: Define principal stress and principal plane.
quiz.a: A principal plane is a plane on which the shear stress is zero. The normal stress on that plane is a principal stress.

quiz.q: Why does an eccentric axial load produce both direct stress and bending stress?
quiz.a: Moving the force to the centroid keeps the same force and adds a moment M = P e. The force at the centroid gives uniform P/A; the moment gives linear M c/I.

quiz.q: A solid shaft of 40 mm diameter carries M = 500 N·m and T = 300 N·m. Find the bending stress, torsional shear stress and σ₁. Use π = 3.142.
A bracket has tensile direct stress 40 MPa and bending stress 90 MPa at one edge. Is the maximum principal stress 130 MPa? Explain.
quiz.a: Only if the shear stress there is zero. With no shear, the normal stresses add on the same plane, giving 130 MPa as a principal stress. With shear, use σ₁ = 65 + √(65² + τ²), which is larger than 130 MPa.

quiz.q: At a point σ<sub>x</sub> = 100 MPa, σ<sub>y</sub> = 40 MPa and τ<sub>xy</sub> = 30 MPa. Find σ₁ and σ₂.
A shaft surface at the neutral axis has zero bending stress but the torque still acts. What are the principal stresses there?
quiz.a: σ<sub>x</sub> = 0 and σ<sub>y</sub> = 0, but τ is not zero. Then σ₁ = τ and σ₂ = −τ; τ<sub>max</sub> = τ.

quiz.q: State the centre and radius of Mohr's circle for plane stress with σ<sub>x</sub>, σ<sub>y</sub> and τ<sub>xy</sub>.
quiz.a: Centre C = ((σ<sub>x</sub> + σ<sub>y</sub>)/2, 0). Radius R = √(((σ<sub>x</sub> − σ<sub>y</sub>)/2)² + τ<sub>xy</sub>²).

beyond: Not for the exam. Principal stresses are the input to fatigue software: a shaft's stress state is computed at every node, then rotated to find the critical plane. Strain rosettes measure three strains on a surface and convert them to principal strains. Search for "principal stress contour", "Mohr's circle strain rosette", and "critical plane fatigue".
